newsitem.title: UK: Sister of UK's Major makes rare political outing.
newsitem.headline: Sister of UK's Major makes rare political outing.

text.p: John Major's biggest fan -- his 67-year-old sister -- brought a homespun touch to the British election campaign on Tuesday with her first newspaper column.
Pat Dessoy, the little-known elder sister of the prime minister, made a rare outing into politics with a column in the Daily Telegraph.

More humdrum than humble, Dessoy revealed that while Major was seeing Queen Elizabeth last week to fix the May 1 election date, she was spending the morning in her south London flat "tidying the kitchen cupboards, rubbing down the paintwork and waiting for the phone to ring".
Dessoy keeps in regular contact with her famous younger brother and Major rang up later to tell her the election news.

In her writing debut, Dessoy says she rarely buys newspapers. "If I want to read something I go to the public library and I get my news from the television on my kitchen table. I frequently turn off the sound if people are talking nonsense, so I can watch how they behave," Dessoy wrote.
Why anyone should be interested in the views of this grey-haired widow, whose sole trip aboard was a three-day visit to Brussels 25 years ago, lies in the riddle of Major himself.

Grey in character as well as appearance, Major, 53, remains a puzzle to much of the British public with his combination of wooden manner, "honest John" image and colourful family background -- his father was once a circus trapeze artist.

In political speeches, Major often draws on his humble background as a young man from the deprived streets of London's Brixton who left school early when the family garden gnome business fell on hard times.

His brother Terry Major-Ball became something of a laughing stock three years ago when he published his own downbeat account of family life with the young man who was turned down for a job as a bus conductor but went on to govern Britain.
Dessoy writes protectively of Major, who has endured personal attacks from both political friends and foes during his 6-1/2 years in office.
"I know how hurt John must be by some of the divisions in his own party. I can understand that one or two people who have lost power may feel bitter...

"Why not retire gracefully instead of sitting there like malevolent toads?" she said. Major's Conservative Party has been ripped apart by divisions over Europe and right-wingers have attacked the premier for weak leadership and lack of conviction.
In a typically understated English put-down, Dessoy dismisses Cherie Blair, the highly-qualified lawyer wife of Labour leader Tony Blair.
"I've decided Mrs Blair isn't quite my cup of tea," she said. Opinion polls show Blair will almost certainly take over from Major as prime minster.
